deep.reconstruction:
The page belongs to Grothendieck's 1983-84 notes on 'systèmes de pseudo-droites', i.e. arrangements of pseudolines in the projective plane. It is a page of combinatorial experiments, not a page of theorems.

(1) Disc model and boundary words. An arrangement of 10 pseudolines, labelled 0,...,9, is drawn in a disc whose boundary circle is the line at infinity (projective plane = disc with antipodal boundary points identified). Pseudoline i has its two ends at boundary points i and i'. For the standard picture (central black/yellow circle) the cyclic order on the boundary is 0 1 2 ... 9 9' 8' ... 0', read along the two half-circles. The written words, such as '3 2 1 0 4 5 6 7 8 9 0' 1' ... 9' | 3 2 1', record this cyclic boundary order as a linear word. The part after '|' repeats the beginning to indicate cyclic wrap-around. Brackets under sub-blocks (e.g. under '0 4 5 6 7 8 9 0' 1' 2' 3'') mark the segment being moved or reversed.

(2) Local move. In the bottom-left diagram three orange pseudolines 1,2,3 cross a green/orange horizontal band. Their order reads '1 2 3' on one side and '3 2 1' on the other. This is the local reversal of a bundle of lines passing through, or near, a common point: a triangle-flip or 'mutation', the Reidemeister-III-type move of pseudoline arrangements. The small top-left sketches (an X; a crossing slid past a green line with a dashed parallel) show the same move with two lines.

(3) Moving a multiple point to infinity. In the large orange disc, lines 1,2,3 are made concurrent at a boundary point, labelled '3 2 1' at the top and '3' 2' 1'' at the bottom. That is, the triple point is pushed onto the line at infinity, making 1,2,3 a 'parallel class'. Shaded triangles mark the cells created or destroyed. The boundary labels are then permuted: 6 and 7 have exchanged their order (…5' 7' 6' 8'… and …4 5 7 6 8 9…). This gives the words '1' 2' 3' 0 4' 5' 7' 6' 8' 9' 0' 3 2 1 | 4 5 7 6 8 9 | 1' 2' 3''. So the page tracks how the cyclic boundary word changes when the line at infinity is moved across vertices of the arrangement, or when a multiple point is moved onto or off it.

(4) Other figures.
- The large grey circle, with arcs marked at 60-degree intervals and arrow marks, appears to indicate the periodicity or identification of the boundary.
- The small bottom circle colours the boundary arcs by blocks (0, 4–9 dark; 1–3 and 1'–3' blue) and draws only lines 1,2,3 as near-parallel chords.
- The red bottom-right diagram shows a bundle of red lines pinched at two multiple points over a green/black horizontal line, with numbered crossing points. It looks like a wiring-diagram / sweep picture: crossings with a horizontal line read off as a sequence of permutations.

This connects with the previous page's axioms for a pair of cellular complexes K, L: 4-valent vertices, each edge of K carrying exactly one vertex of L, and a face-counting identity. Overall the goal seems to be a combinatorial (word or permutation) encoding of pseudoline arrangements and of the elementary moves between them.
errors: No outright errors are detectable; the page is exploratory. In the second word the crossed-out '6' and overwritten '7 6' show the 6/7 order being corrected in real time. The orange disc is hand-drawn and its cell structure cannot be fully verified against the words.

ideas.what: Encoding a projective pseudoline arrangement by the cyclic order of line ends on the boundary circle (line at infinity)
ideas.modern_name: boundary/cyclic order of an arrangement; local sequences; circular sequences of permutations

ideas.what: Local reversal of a bundle of lines through a (near-)multiple point: order 1 2 3 becomes 3 2 1
ideas.modern_name: triangle flip / mutation (Ringel's homotopy theorem); a move in allowable sequences

ideas.what: Moving a multiple point onto the line at infinity (making lines parallel) and tracking the change of boundary word
ideas.modern_name: change of the line at infinity / reorientation-type operations on rank-3 oriented matroids; sweeping

ideas.what: Wiring-diagram style picture of lines crossing a horizontal sweep line, with multiple points
ideas.modern_name: wiring diagrams / sweep of pseudoline arrangements

missed.claim: This is a documentary record that Grothendieck, around 1983-84, was independently working with the combinatorics of pseudoline arrangements: boundary cyclic words, triangle flips, and moving points to infinity. This parallels Goodman–Pollack's allowable sequences and the rank-3 oriented-matroid literature, and there is no sign he knew of them. Nothing on this page goes mathematically beyond that literature.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is of historical interest for the (little-studied) pseudoline/'géométrie modérée' strand of his 1980s work, not a new result.

deep.surprise_reason: These are hand experiments with standard pseudoline-arrangement combinatorics: boundary words, triple-point flips, and parallel classes at infinity. Interesting only as evidence of Grothendieck's independent rediscovery of known tools; no new theorem or construction is visible.
transcription_corrections: The '0' in the word '1'2'3'0 4'5'…' is unprimed: it is the end of line 0, as completeness of the 20 labels requires.
The top word begins '3 2 1 0' with the 3 overwritten. The bracket beneath spans roughly '0 4 5 6 7 8 9 0' 1' 2' 3'', with an extra pencil sub-bracket.
Orange disc boundary labels: top '3 2 1' (concurrent), left '5', '4', '7', '8', '9'; right '9'', '8'', '6'', '7'', '5'', '4''; bottom '3' 2' 1'' (concurrent).
The second word reads '… 3 2 1 | 4 5 [-6-] 7 6 8 9 | 1'2'3'', with a large overwritten '6' near '7 6'.
The bottom-left diagram has '1 2 3' above the crossing and '3 2 1' below it.
